input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-262: Introduction to Computer Science Theory. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course provides an introduction to the theory of computation, including formal languages, grammars, auto-mata theory, computability, and complexity. Prerequisites: (MATH-190 or MATH-200) and (CSCI-140 or CSCI-141 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-123 or SWEN-124 or CSECI-123 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-123 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[mit-algorithms]
Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.

[opendsa]
OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.

[rit-csci-262]
This course provides an introduction to the theory of computation, including formal languages, grammars, auto-mata theory, computability, and complexity. Prerequisites: (MATH-190 or MATH-200) and (CSCI-140 or CSCI-141 or CSCI-242 or SWEN-123 or SWEN-124 or CSECI-123 or CSEC-124 or GCIS-123 or GCIS-124 or GCIS-127) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: Computer science theory models computation using formal languages and automata to define what can be computed and how efficiently.
beats.example: A finite automaton accepts the string 'abab' by transitioning through states that track alternating 'a' and 'b' characters.
beats.title: Foundations of Computation
beats.visualDirection: Display a state diagram with labeled transitions for a DFA that accepts alternating 'a' and 'b' strings, highlighting the start and accept states.

beats.claim: Formal languages are sets of strings generated by grammars, which provide a rigorous syntax for describing computational inputs.
beats.example: A context-free grammar defines valid arithmetic expressions by recursively combining terms and operators.
beats.title: Formal Languages and Grammars
beats.visualDirection: Show a parse tree for the expression '3 + 4 * 2' with labeled non-terminals and terminal nodes.

beats.claim: Automata are mathematical machines that process input strings and accept or reject them based on defined transition rules.
beats.example: A pushdown automaton recognizes nested parentheses by pushing symbols onto a stack and popping them during matching.
beats.title: Automata Theory Basics
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a pushdown automaton with a stack diagram showing push/pop operations during parenthesis matching.

beats.claim: Computability theory determines which problems can be solved by any algorithm, establishing fundamental boundaries of computation.
beats.example: The halting problem demonstrates that no general algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary program will eventually stop.
beats.title: Computability Limits
beats.visualDirection: Present a flowchart showing the decision tree for the halting problem, ending in an undecidable branch.

beats.claim: Complexity theory classifies algorithms by their time and space requirements, using asymptotic notation to describe growth rates.
beats.example: A sorting algorithm with O(n log n) time complexity processes larger inputs more efficiently than O(n^2) alternatives.
beats.title: Complexity and Resource Bounds
beats.visualDirection: Plot two curves on a log-log graph comparing O(n log n) and O(n^2) growth, labeling the axes and intersection point.

beats.claim: Loop invariants are properties that remain true before and after each iteration, enabling formal verification of algorithm correctness.
beats.example: In a binary search, the invariant states that the target value, if present, lies within the current search interval.
beats.title: Loop Invariants and Proofs
beats.visualDirection: Show a table tracking the search interval bounds and the invariant statement across three iterations of binary search.

beats.claim: Divide-and-conquer algorithms break problems into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, and combine results to form the final solution.
beats.example: Merge sort splits an array into halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves into a complete sorted array.
beats.title: Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
beats.visualDirection: Display a recursive tree diagram showing array splits and merge steps for a 4-element array.

beats.claim: Recurrence relations mathematically describe the cost of recursive algorithms, allowing precise calculation of time complexity.
beats.example: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) describes the time complexity of merge sort, solving to O(n log n).
beats.title: Recurrence Relations
beats.visualDirection: Show a recurrence tree with labeled nodes for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn, summing the work at each level.

beats.claim: Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to solve reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path problems efficiently.
beats.example: Breadth-first search finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph by exploring neighbors level by level.
beats.title: Graph Algorithms and Reachability
beats.visualDirection: Render a directed graph with BFS traversal order highlighted, showing visited nodes and edge directions.

beats.claim: A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space to ensure robust algorithmic design.
beats.example: Before implementing a sorting routine, verify the preconditions, prove the loop invariant, and derive the recurrence for time bounds.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: List a three-step checklist: 1) Define inputs/outputs, 2) Prove correctness via invariants, 3) Analyze complexity with recurrences.

learningObjectives: Define formal languages and automata as mathematical models for computation.
Explain how loop invariants and divide-and-conquer strategies structure algorithmic proofs.
Apply asymptotic notation and recurrence relations to analyze resource bounds of recursive algorithms.
